column2: Among these aspirants (murīdūn) of the Sufis are a group of simpletons (bahālīl), feeble-minded people, more like the insane than the sane. Yet for all that, the stations of sainthood and the states of the truthful (ṣiddīqūn) hold good for them, and whoever among the people of spiritual taste understands them knows this from their states, although they are not under religious obligation (taklīf). Marvels occur to them in their reports about hidden things, because they are bound by nothing, so they give free rein to their speech on these matters and bring forth marvels from it. Jurists sometimes deny that they hold any of the stations, because they see that obligation has lapsed for them, while sainthood is attained only through worship. This is a mistake, for God’s favor is something He gives to whom He wills, and the attainment of sainthood does not depend on worship or on anything else. Since the human soul has firmly established existence, God the Exalted singles it out for whatever He wills of His gifts. The rational souls of these people have not been lost, nor have they been corrupted as is the case with the insane; what they have lost is only the intellect on which obligation hinges. This is an attribute special to the soul, and it consists of necessary knowledge belonging to man, by which his thinking is sharpened and he knows the conditions of his livelihood and the right ordering of his household. It is as though, once he can discern the conditions of his livelihood and the right ordering of his household, no excuse remains to him regarding the acceptance of obligations for the sake of setting right his life to come. One who lacks this attribute has not lost his soul, nor is he oblivious of his reality, such that his reality would exist while he lacks the intellect of obligation, which is knowledge of livelihood; and there is nothing impossible in that,

and God’s choosing of His servants for gnosis (maʿrifa) does not depend on any of the obligations. Once that is established, know that the state of these people may be confused with that of the insane, whose rational souls are corrupted and who join the beasts. You have signs by which to tell them apart. One is that you find in these simpletons no direction at all. Another is that they are created simple-minded from the very beginning of their growth, whereas madness befalls the insane after some time of life through natural bodily accidents; when this befalls them and their rational souls are corrupted, they go away empty-handed. Another is how much they act upon people, for good and for ill, because they do not wait for permission, there being no obligation in their case, whereas the insane have no such action. This is a section to which our discussion has brought us, and God is the guide to what is right.

Some people claim that there are means of perceiving the unseen here without any withdrawal from the senses. Among them are the astrologers, who hold to astral indications, to what the positions of the stars in the celestial sphere entail, to their effects on the elements, and to the mixture that arises between their natures through their mutual aspects and is conveyed by that mixture to the air. These astrologers have nothing to do with the unseen: theirs are only intuitive conjectures and surmises built on the effects of the stars and the mixture they produce in the air, together with further intuition by which the observer arrives at its details in the individuals of the world, as Ptolemy said. We shall show the invalidity of that in its place, God willing; and even if it were established, its utmost is intuition and surmise, and it has nothing to do with what we have mentioned. Among these are a group of the common people who devised, for drawing out the unseen and learning of events, a craft they called khaṭṭ al-raml (“drawing in the sand”), after the material in which they do their work. The substance of this craft is that they made out of dots figures of four ranks, which differ as their ranks differ in evenness and oddness and in being alike in them. The figures came to sixteen, for if the ranks are all even or all odd, there are two figures; if the odd is in one rank only, four figures; if the odd is in two ranks, six figures; and if it is in three ranks, four figures. So sixteen figures resulted, and they distinguished all of them by their names and kinds into fortunate and unfortunate, as the planets are,

and they assigned to them sixteen houses, natural by their claim, as if they were the twelve signs of the zodiac of the celestial sphere and the four angles (awtād), and they gave each figure a house, lines, and an indication of a class of the existing things of the world of the elements peculiar to it. From this they devised an art with which they imitated the art of astrology and its kind of judgment. But the judgments of astrology rest on natural positions, as Ptolemy claims, whereas these rest only on arbitrary stipulations and chance whims, and no proof stands behind any of them. They claim that its origin lies in the ancient prophecies in the world, and they sometimes attribute it to Daniel or to Idrīs, God’s blessings be upon them both, as is done with all the crafts. They sometimes claim that it is lawful, and cite as proof the Prophet’s saying, God bless him and grant him peace: “There was a prophet who used to draw lines; whoever’s lines agree with his, that is it.” But there is nothing in the hadith to show that drawing in the sand is lawful, as is claimed by some who have no real understanding, because the meaning of the hadith is that there was a prophet who used to draw lines, and revelation would come to him at that drawing; and it is not impossible that this was the habit of some of the prophets. So whoever’s lines agreed with that prophet’s, “that is it”, that is, it is sound among drawings, through the revelation that supported it for that prophet, whose habit was that revelation came to him at the drawing. But if it is taken from the drawing alone, without the agreement of a revelation, then no. This is the meaning of the hadith, and God knows best.

When they wish to draw out something hidden, as they claim, they set about with a sheet of paper, or sand, or flour, and put down dots in lines, according to the number of the four ranks. Then they repeat that four times, so that sixteen lines result. Then they cancel the dots in pairs and put what remains of each line, whether a pair or a single, in its rank in order, so that four figures result, which they set in a row one after another. Then they generate from them four more figures, from the side of the breadth, taking into account each rank and what faces it in the figure opposite it, and what results from the two of them, pair or single; so there are eight figures set in a row. Then from each two figures they generate a figure beneath them, taking into account likewise what results in each rank of the two figures, pair or single; so there are four more beneath them. Then from the four they generate two figures beneath them in the same way, and from the two a figure beneath them in the same way; then from this fifteenth figure together with the first figure they generate a figure, which is the last of the sixteen. Then they pass judgment on the whole drawing according to what its figures entail of fortune and misfortune, by essence, aspect, occupancy and combination, and by indication of the classes of existing things, and all the rest, with strange arbitrariness. This craft became widespread in civilization, and treatises were composed on it, and there became famous

in it eminent figures of earlier and later times; yet, as you have seen, it is arbitrariness and whim. The verified truth that should be before your mind is that unseen things are never perceived by any craft, and there is no way to know them except for the special few among mankind who are innately disposed to return from the world of sense to the world of spirit. For that reason the astrologers call this whole class “Venusians” (zuhriyyūn), after what the indication of Venus at the root of their nativities, by their claim, entails as to perception of the unseen. As for drawing in the sand and the other arts of this kind: if the one who looks into it belongs to those with this special property, and what he intends by these things he looks at, whether dots, bones or other things, is to occupy the senses so that the soul may return for a moment to the world of spiritual beings, then it belongs with ṭarq with pebbles, looking into the hearts of animals, and into transparent mirrors, as we have mentioned. But if he is not so, and intends instead to know the unseen by this craft, believing that it gives him that, then it is idle babble in word and deed; and God guides whom He wills.

The sign of this innate disposition with which the people of this perception of the unseen are created is that, when they turn to learning about events, they are seized by a departure from their natural state, such as yawning, stretching, and the first signs of withdrawal from the senses; this varies in strength and weakness according to the degree to which it is present in them. Whoever does not show this sign has no part in the perception of the unseen; he is merely striving to put his lie into circulation.
Section

Among them are groups who lay down rules for drawing out the unseen that are not of the first stage, which belongs to the faculties of perception of the spiritual soul, nor of the intuition built on the effects of the stars as Ptolemy claimed, nor of the conjecture and surmise that the diviners work with. They are rather sophistries that they set up like traps for people of weak minds. I mention of them only what authors have mentioned and what the elite have been fond of. Among those rules is the reckoning they call ḥisāb al-nīm, which is mentioned at the end of the Kitāb al-siyāsa (“The Book of Politics”) attributed to Aristotle, and by which one learns which of two warring kings is the victor and which the vanquished. It is this: you reckon the letters in the name of one of them by the jummal reckoning, the system agreed upon for the letters of abjad, from one up to 1,000, as units, tens, hundreds and thousands. When you have reckoned the name and obtained a number from it, reckon the name of the other in the same way. Then subtract nines from each of them, nine at a time, and keep the remainder of this one and the remainder of that one. Then look at the two numbers remaining from the reckoning of the two names. If the two numbers differ in quantity and both are even or both are odd, the one with the smaller is the victor. If one is even and the other odd, the one with the larger is the victor. If they are equal in quantity and both are even, the one pursued is the victor; and if both are odd, the pursuer is the victor. Two verses on this operation are recited that are well known among people, namely:

I see that among the evens and the odds the smallest of them rises ... and the greatest of them, when they are allied, is the victor / The one pursued wins when the evens are equal ... and when the odds are equal, the pursuer wins

Then, to find what remains of the letters after subtracting nines from them, they set a rule well known among them for the subtraction of nines. They gathered the letters denoting one in the four ranks, which are (alif), denoting one; (yāʾ), denoting ten, since it is one in the rank of the tens; (qāf), denoting 100, since it is one in the rank of the hundreds; and (shīn), denoting 1,000, since it is one in the rank of the thousands. After the thousand there is no number that a letter denotes, because shīn is the last of the letters of abjad. Then they arranged these four letters in the order of the ranks, and a four-letter word came out of them, which is (ayqsh). Then they did the same with the letters denoting two in the three ranks, and dropped the rank of the thousands from them, because it was the last of the letters of abjad; so the total of the letters for two in the three ranks was three letters,

which are (bāʾ), denoting two among the units; (kāf), denoting two among the tens, which is twenty; and (rāʾ), denoting two among the hundreds, which is 200. They made of them a single three-letter word in the order of the ranks, which is bkr. Then they did the same with the letters denoting three, and from them arose the word jls, and so on to the end of the letters of abjad. There came to be nine words, reaching the end of the count of the units, which are ayqsh bkr jls dmt hnth wṣkh zʿdh ḥfẓ ṭḍgh, arranged in the succession of the numbers, and each word has the number whose rank it occupies: one for the word ayqsh, two for the word bkr, three for the word jls, and so on to the ninth, which is ṭḍgh, which has nine. So when they want to subtract nines from a name, they look up each letter of it to see in which of these words it falls, and take the number of that word in its place. Then they add up the numbers they take in place of the letters of the name; if the sum exceeds nine, they take what is left over beyond it, and if not, they take it as it is. Then they do the same with the other name, and compare the two results as we have set out. The secret of this is clear: what remains of each round number among the numbers, once nines are subtracted, is simply one, so it is as if one added up only the count of the round numbers in each rank,

so that the counts of the round numbers came to be like units, and there is no difference between the 2, the 20, the 200 and the 2,000: all of them are two; and likewise the 3, the 30, the 300 and the 3,000 are all three. So the numbers were set in succession, standing only for the counts of the round numbers and nothing else, and the letters denoting the kinds of round numbers, units, tens, hundreds and thousands, were put in each word, and the number assigned to the word came to stand for each letter in it, whether it denoted units, tens or hundreds. So the number of each word is taken in place of the letters in it, and all of them are added up to the end, as we have said. This is the procedure that has been current among people from of old. Some of our teachers whom we met held that the correct ones here are nine other words in place of these, arranged in succession like them, and they do with them in subtracting nines exactly what they do with the others. They are these: arb ystmk jzlṭ mdwṣ hf tḥdhn ʿsh khʿ thḍẓ, nine words in the order of the numbers, each having the number whose rank it occupies. Among them are three-letter, four-letter and two-letter words, and they do not follow a consistent principle, as you can see; but our teachers transmitted them from the master of the Maghrib in these branches of knowledge, sīmiyāʾ, the secrets of the letters, and astrology, namely Abū al-ʿAbbās ibn al-Bannāʾ,

and they say of him that working with these words in the subtraction of nines in the ḥisāb al-nīm is more correct than working with the ayqsh words; God knows how that is. All of these are means of perceiving the unseen; [the book] is not ascribed to Aristotle by the verifying scholars, because of the opinions in it that are far from verification and proof; going through it will bear this out for you, if you are among those firmly grounded. Among these artificial rules for drawing out unseen things, as they claim, is the zāʾiraja called “Zāʾirajat al-ʿālam” (“The Zāʾiraja of the World”), ascribed to Abū al-ʿAbbās, Sīdī Aḥmad al-Sabtī, one of the eminent Sufis of the Maghrib, who lived in Marrakesh at the end of the sixth century [AH], in the time of Abū Yaʿqūb al-Manṣūr, one of the Almohad kings. It is a strange craft in its working. Many of the elite are fond of getting the unseen from it by its well-known, riddling operation, and so they are eager to solve its code and uncover its obscurity.

Its form, in which the operation is carried out among them, is a great circle, inside which are parallel circles for the celestial spheres, the elements, the generated things, the spiritual beings, and other kinds of created things and sciences. Each circle is divided into the divisions of its sphere, either the signs of the zodiac, or the elements, or others, and the lines of each division run to the center; they call them the chords (awtār). On each chord are placed successive letters. Among them are the barāshīm of the zimām, which are the shapes of the numbers among the people of the government registers and of arithmetic in the Maghrib at the present time, and among them are the barāshīm of the dust (ghubār) familiar in the interior of the zāʾiraja. Between the circles are the names of the sciences and the places of the generated things. On the outside of the circles is a table of many cells crossing lengthwise and breadthwise, containing fifty-five cells in width and 131 in length; parts of it have their cells filled, sometimes with numbers and sometimes with letters, and parts have empty cells. The relation of those numbers in their positions is not known, nor the division that determined which cells are filled and which are empty. Around the edges of the zāʾiraja are verses in the ṭawīl meter, with lām voweled with a as the rhyme letter, which contain the manner of working to draw the sought answer out of that zāʾiraja, but they are in the nature of riddles, lacking plainness and clarity. On some sides of the zāʾiraja is a line of verse attributed to one of the great authorities on prognostication in the Maghrib, namely Mālik ibn Wuhayb, one of the scholars of Seville, who lived under the Lamtūnī dynasty, and this is the text of the verse.
A question great in creation: you have won it, so guard it then ... strange things of doubt, whose mastery is earnestness, for example

This is the verse in current use among them in the operation for drawing the answer out of the question in this zāʾiraja and others. When they want to draw out the answer to what is asked about among questions, they write down that question and break it into letters. Then they take the ascendant for that time from the signs of the zodiac and their degrees, and they go to the zāʾiraja, then to the chord in it that borders the rising sign at its beginning, running to the center and then to the circumference of the circle opposite the ascendant. They take all the letters written on it from its beginning to its end, and the numbers marked between them, and turn them into letters by the jummal reckoning. Sometimes they shift their units to tens and their tens to hundreds, and the reverse in both cases, as the rule of operation among them requires. They put them with the letters of the question, and add to this everything on the chord that borders the third sign from the ascendant, of letters and numbers, from its beginning to the center only, not passing beyond it to the circumference; they do with the numbers what they did with the first, and add them to the other letters. Then they break up the letters of the verse, which is the basis of the operation and its rule among them, namely the verse of Mālik ibn Wuhayb mentioned above, and put them aside. Then they multiply the number of the degrees of the ascendant by the exponent (uss) of the sign, and its exponent among them is the distance of the sign from the end of the ranks, the opposite of what the exponent is among the people of the craft of arithmetic,

for among them it is the distance from the first of the ranks. Then they multiply it by another number they call the greater exponent and the basic cycle (al-dawr al-aṣlī), and with what has been gathered for them from that they enter the cells of the table, according to known rules, stated procedures and counted cycles. They extract letters from them and drop others, set what they have against the letters of the verse, and transfer from it what they transfer to the letters of the question and what goes with them. Then they strike out those letters by known numbers that they call the cycles (adwār), and in each cycle they take out the letter at which the cycle ends. They repeat that for the number of cycles fixed among them for this, so that at the end separate letters come out, and they are put together in succession and become words composed in a single verse, in the meter and rhyme of the verse against which the operation is set, which is the verse of Mālik ibn Wuhayb mentioned above, as we shall set out all of this in the chapter on the sciences, on the manner of working with this zāʾiraja. We have seen many of the elite throw themselves at drawing out the unseen from it by those operations, thinking that the agreement of the answer with the question in the concordance of the discourse is proof of agreement with reality. That is not correct, because it has already been shown to you that the unseen is never perceived by anything artificial. The agreement in it between answer and question is only in terms of intelligibility and concordance of the discourse, so that the answer is coherent or fitting for the question,

and the occurrence of that in this craft, through the breaking up of the letters gathered from the question and the chords, the entering of the table with the numbers gathered from multiplying the assumed numbers, the extraction of letters from the table by that, the striking out of others, the repetition of that in the counted cycles, and the setting of all of it against the letters of the verse in succession, is not implausible. Some intelligent people may become aware of a proportion among these things, and so come to know the unknown. For proportion among things is the cause of arriving at the unknown from the known that is present to the soul, and a way to arriving at it, especially for the people of spiritual exercise, since it gives the intellect strength in analogical reasoning and an increase in thought; the explanation of that has been given more than once. It is for this reason that they mostly ascribe this zāʾiraja to people of spiritual exercise: it is ascribed to al-Sabtī, and I have come across another ascribed to Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allāh. Upon my life, it is among the strange operations and wondrous labors. As for the answer that comes out of it, the secret of its coming out in verse, as it appears to me, is only the comparison with the letters of that verse, which is why the verse comes out in its meter and rhyme. What points to this is that we have found other operations of theirs of this kind in which they dropped the comparison with the verse, and the answer did not come out in verse, as you will see when we discuss that in its place. Many people’s faculties of perception are too narrow to believe in this operation and its reaching what is sought,

so that he denies its validity and thinks it is among imaginings and illusions, and that the one who works it fixes the letters of the verse he is composing as he wishes among the letters of the question and the chords, and carries out those operations without proportion or rule, then comes forth with the verse and gives the impression that the operation came about by a regulated method. This thought is a false fancy, brought on by falling short of understanding the proportion between existing and non-existing things and the disparity between faculties of perception and intellects. But it is in the nature of every perceiver to deny what lies beyond his capacity to perceive. To refute this it is enough for us to have witnessed the working of this craft, and to have decisive intuition, for it comes with a consistent operation and a sound rule, about which there is no doubt for one who engages in it and has intelligence and intuition. If many a puzzle in number, which is the clearest of the clear, is hard for understanding to grasp because the proportion in it is remote and hidden, what do you think of a matter like this, where the proportion is hidden and strange as well? Let us then give a puzzle problem by which something of what we have said will become clear to you. Its example: if you were told, “Take a number of dirhams, and put opposite each dirham three fulūs (copper coins); then gather the fulūs you have taken and buy a bird with them; then buy birds with all the dirhams at the price of that bird; how many are the birds bought with the dirhams?” its answer is that you say they are nine, because you know that

the fulūs of a dirham are twenty-four, and that three is an eighth of it, and that the number of eighths of one is eight. So when you add the eighth from the dirhams to the other eighth, and all of it is the price of a bird, there are eight birds, the number of eighths of one, and you add to the eight another bird, which is the one bought with the fulūs taken first, and at whose price you bought with the dirhams; so there are nine. You see how the implicit answer came out for you through the secret of the proportion between the numbers of the problem, whereas estimation (al-wahm), when this and its like are first put before you, only places it in the category of the unseen that cannot be known. And it is clear that proportion among things is what brings out the unknown of them from the known; and this holds only for occurrences that have already come about in existence or in knowledge. As for future events, when the causes of their occurrence are not known and no true report about them is established, they are an unseen that cannot be known. Once that is clear to you, all the operations performed in the zāʾiraja serve only to draw the answer out of the wording of the question, because, as you have seen, they derive letters in one order from those very letters in another order, and the secret of that is only a proportion between the two, which some perceive and others do not. Whoever knows that proportion finds it easy to draw out that answer by those rules,

and the answer indicates, in another respect, by what its words and constructions signify by convention, the occurrence of one of the two sides of the question, negation or affirmation. This does not belong to the first respect, but goes back to the agreement of the speech with what is in external reality, and there is no way to know that from these operations; rather, humans are veiled from it, and God has reserved its knowledge to Himself; “God knows and you do not know” (2: 216).
